extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, communications teams, marketers, and people writing press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing, formatting, placing, and attributing quotes inside press releases so they are media-friendly, engaging, and likely to be picked up by journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Every quote should be enclosed in double quotation marks to clearly distinguish it from the rest of the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “Our new product presents a breakthrough in sustainable technology,” said Jill Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute your quotes (full name, title, organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the quote, attribute it to the speaker with their full name, title and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “This milestone will revolutionize the industry,” said Jill Smith, CEO of AgroSphere. Use the standard attribution format (e.g., 'said [Name], [Title] of [Organization]').

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow AP Style guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere to Associated Press style guidelines for punctuation, capitalization and attribution to make quotes media-friendly and ready for direct use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using AP style ensures consistency and makes it easier for journalists to lift quotes verbatim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break up long quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: If a quote is too long, break it into two smaller quotes with attribution in between.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the first sentence as a strong, standalone statement and follow with a second sentence that builds on it. Example format in the page shows an attribution between two quoted sentences to improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use block format for longer quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: For quotes longer than three lines, use a block quote format by indenting the entire quote for visual separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Block quotes help maintain readability and increase visibility for longer statements, useful for readers who scan announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider using pull quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off a strong quote using a larger font or a text box (pull quote) to draw attention and make it more powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR Newswire offers pull quotes free of charge with US1 distribution; use this sparingly to highlight especially strong soundbites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place quotes at the beginning to grab attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing a quote at the beginning hooks the reader, sets the tone, adds human perspective and gives journalists a strong soundbite early on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use beginning placement when announcing major milestones (mergers, launches), sharing provocative executive statements, or introducing a new vision or strategic direction. Example: “This achievement marks a turning point for our industry,” said Jill Smith, CEO of AgroSphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place quotes in the middle to support key messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Position a quote after you’ve introduced main details to back up claims and add insight to factual information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Middle placement reinforces claims with partner/customer/executive statements, provides expert analysis, and adds human context once readers have context. Example: customer testimonial-style quote used after product details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place quotes at the end to leave a lasting impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a closing quote to create a strong final statement that reinforces a call-to-action, future vision, or final takeaway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End placement is appropriate for addressing future goals, reinforcing CTAs, or closing with inspirational, forward-looking language. Example: “This is just the beginning,” added Jill Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get quotes from the right people
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute quotes to influential or authoritative voices to boost credibility and visibility; consider executives, customers, partners, employees, or industry experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive quotes highlight strategy/vision; customer quotes show real-world impact; partner quotes emphasize collaboration. Also aim for diverse voices across ages, genders and ethnic backgrounds to broaden appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep quotes conversational
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes should sound like something a real person would say in conversation — avoid polished language, technical or corporate jargon and buzzwords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: “Our proprietary, market-leading, AI-enabled platform leverages cutting-edge innovation to drive unparalleled efficiency.” Better: “This new technology helps companies work smarter, faster and much more efficiently.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise (one to two sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists prefer short, punchy quotes they can use as-is; stick with one to two sentences and remove unnecessary words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long-winded quotes that rehash details. Anti-pattern example given and a concise replacement offered. Focus on clear statements and brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include forward-looking statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes about the company’s plans or future potential signal growth, ambition and relevance and are more likely to draw attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use emotional language that triggers enthusiasm and highlights future potential. Example: “This partnership is a game-changer for our industry. It opens doors for innovation and customer impact...”

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer insight, not repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release quote should bring a fresh perspective or emotional insight instead of rehashing information already stated in the announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid restating the obvious (e.g., avoid 'Today marks the launch of our new product'). Prefer impact statements (e.g., 'Today’s launch marks a new era for our company').

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of quotes (quality over quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can use multiple quotes, but try to limit them to one or two key voices that add unique perspectives; too many quotes can clutter the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists prefer a few powerful soundbites over many unremarkable statements; prioritize the most authoritative or insightful voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test whether a quote is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If removing a quote leaves the core message intact, the quote may not be necessary and can be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this simple test to determine if a quote adds value (personality, insight, credibility) or merely fills space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting specifics: do not italicize; use block for 3+ sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: According to AP style referenced on the page, quotes are enclosed in double quotation marks and are not italicized; if a quote is three sentences or more, use a block quote format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAQ guidance: use double quotes normally; reserve block quote formatting for longer multi-sentence quotations to aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quotes media-ready (ready-to-use soundbites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft quotes so journalists can lift them verbatim — clear, punchy soundbites increase chances of media pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for one- to two-sentence statements that encapsulate key messages, emotion and relevance; provide examples of effective quotes used in real press releases on the page.
